podcast.body: Produced by longtime collaborator Tony Visconti, this melodic album was hailed by critics as David Bowie's strongest since "Scary Monsters" and marked a significant "return to form." It reached number 14 on the Billboard 200, representing his best album chart showing in nearly two decades, and made the top five in the UK, sparking his early 2000s comeback. "The Melodic Heathen in 2002 sparked the comeback."

podcast.body: Released in June 2002, this album marked Bowie's first collaboration with producer Tony Visconti since 1980, following a 20-year silence between them. It adopted a 70s-era art rock/art pop feel, incorporating dystopianism and dread reminiscent of albums like *Ziggy Stardust*, *Aladdin Sane*, *Diamond Dogs*, and *Station to Station*. The album was deeply affected by the 9/11 attacks, the birth of his daughter Alexandria, and the death of his beloved mother. Critics hailed it as his best work since *Scary Monsters* 22 years prior, reaching number 14 in the US (his best since 1984's *Tonight*), number 9 in Canada, and number 5 in the UK. "The whole thing was a welcome return to form."

podcast.body: This album marked a return to consistent musical output for Bowie in the early 2000s, suggesting he had no intention of stopping his recording career. "Meanwhile, Bowie continued to make records. There was heathen in 2002."
